https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04567:
Mean Reversion Exit Rules in ETF Markets

Abstract: We study the exit side of short-horizon mean reversion strategies in exchange traded funds, a question that has received far less attention than entry signal construction. Using daily closing prices for a broad cross section of US listed equity ETFs over the period 1999 to 2022, we compare fixed horizon exits, threshold based exits on the relative strength index, and volatility scaled stop rules. We find that the distribution of holding periods is strongly right skewed: the median profitable position closes within four trading days, while a small minority of positions remain open long enough to dominate realized drawdown. Imposing a hard maximum holding period of ten trading days removes most of that tail without materially reducing gross returns. We further document that exit rule choice interacts with execution cost assumptions. Under a round trip cost of five basis points the ranking of exit rules is stable, but at twenty basis points the threshold exits underperform the fixed horizon exits because they trade more often. Our results are robust to subperiod splits and to excluding the most illiquid quintile of funds. We report all parameter choices and provide the full set of trial configurations examined, including those that were discarded.

Subjects: Trading and Market Microstructure; Portfolio Management

Momentum Exit Rules and Holding Periods

Most of the published work on momentum and short horizon mean reversion spends its energy on the entry condition and treats the exit as an afterthought. In this post we run the opposite experiment: we hold the entry rule fixed and vary only the exit. The entry is a simple one, a two period relative strength index reading below twenty at the close, executed on the following open so there is no lookahead. Against that fixed entry we test four exits. The first is a fixed horizon exit after n trading days. The second closes the position when the relative strength index recovers above a threshold. The third is a volatility scaled stop placed at a multiple of average true range. The fourth combines the threshold exit with a hard maximum holding period. Across the full sample the combined rule produced the most stable distribution of outcomes, largely because the maximum holding period truncates the left tail that the threshold exit alone leaves open. We want to be careful about what this does and does not show. It is a single entry rule on a single universe, the cost assumptions are fixed at a level that suits a retail account, and we have not adjusted for the number of configurations examined. Treat the holding period result as a hypothesis worth testing on your own data rather than as a finding.
